stem.en: A farmer sees round, tumour-like swellings on the stems of some plants in her field. A plant scientist says it is crown gall disease. What causes these swellings?

text.en: Water collecting under the outer layer of the stem, which makes the stem puff up like a blister.

feedback.en: No. The swellings are not water. They are made of many new cells formed by fast cell division.

text.en: Insects laying their eggs inside the stem, so that the young insects grow inside the swelling.

feedback.en: No. Crown gall disease is caused by a bacterium, not by insects.

text.en: Old cells in the stem growing larger and larger, without any new cells being formed at all.

feedback.en: No. The swellings form because cells divide rapidly, so a great many new cells are made.

text.en: A bacterium, Agrobacterium tumefaciens, which leads to rapid and uncontrolled cell division.

feedback.en: Yes. The bacterium causes the stem cells to divide rapidly and without control, and the swellings form.

explanation.en: Crown gall disease is caused by the bacterium Agrobacterium tumefaciens. Cells in the stem divide rapidly and without control, and this forms the tumour-like swellings. Scientists studied how this bacterium passes its genetic material into plant cells, and now use it to put useful genes into plants.

hints.en: Are the swellings made of water, of insects, or of many new cells?
